analysis.one_liner: Bars bankruptcy courts from shielding corporate owners and executives from government lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in July 2021 with one cosponsor and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company files for bankruptcy, some courts currently release the company's owners, officers, and directors from liability as part of the bankruptcy plan — a practice the courts themselves disagree on. This bill would stop bankruptcy courts from doing that when the lawsuits come from a state, a city, a federally recognized tribe, or the federal government. It is named for the Sackler family, whose company's bankruptcy proposed just such a release of their opioid liability.
analysis.who_benefits: State, local, and tribal governments and federal agencies that sue corporations would keep their right to pursue a company's owners and executives even if the company itself goes bankrupt. People who depend on those lawsuits for accountability and compensation — for example, communities harmed by the opioid crisis — benefit from governments keeping that leverage. Bankruptcy victims outside government would also gain from the limits on the practice.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Governments suing corporations, and mass-tort victims

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends bankruptcy law so a court cannot release or enjoin claims against a non-debtor — a company's owners, officers, or directors — when those claims are brought by a state, municipality, federally recognized tribe, or the United States.

It closes off the arrangement its name points to: a company files bankruptcy, its owners pay a negotiated sum, and the court wipes out the owners' own liability to government plaintiffs. The bill's short title — the SACKLER Act — is aimed at that practice, which a circuit split among the courts has left legally unsettled.
It is not a total freeze: a bankruptcy court may still pause such lawsuits for up to 90 days, so the bankruptcy case itself can proceed without the owners being sued mid-case.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy owners, officers, and directors of companies facing large government lawsuits — most directly the Sackler family, the bill's namesake — would lose the ability to buy peace from those claims through their company's bankruptcy. Companies would also find it harder to attract owners willing to contribute settlement money if the owners stay exposed to suit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wealthy corporate owners and executives facing lawsuits

drawbacks.text: Third-party releases are often the price for getting owners to contribute money to a bankruptcy estate: if owners know they will remain exposed to government lawsuits, they may contribute less or refuse to settle at all, leaving victims with a smaller recovery. The CRS summary notes courts allow the practice partly to carry out bankruptcy plans, and it is what made large settlements possible in complex cases.

The bill is narrow: it protects only claims brought by governments. Claims by private plaintiffs — individual victims, hospitals, insurers — could still be released against non-debtors, so many people harmed by a company would not get the same protection.

It resolves an unsettled area of law by taking the option off the table entirely, in every case, rather than letting judges weigh whether a release is fair and whether the owners' payment justifies it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: it keeps governments' most powerful lever — the threat of suing a company's owners personally — intact when a company tries to use bankruptcy to make the claims disappear. But the cost case is serious and honest supporters should admit it: releases are often the mechanism that pulls billions out of owners' pockets for victims, and if owners refuse to pay without a release, victims can end up worse off. The bill's narrow scope — leaving private plaintiffs exposed — also undercuts its own logic. On balance it favors accountability over settlement convenience, at a genuine risk to settlement size.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in July 2021 and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on July 26, 2021, joined by Senator Warren as its only cosponsor.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never held a hearing or vote, and the bill died there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and executives of companies facing mass lawsuits — the Sackler family most directly, as the bill's namesake — are better off, because bankruptcy courts kept the power to release their claims and the threat of a statutory ban was never realized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate owners shielding wealth from lawsuits

sides.party_line_note: Both of the bill's supporters were Democrats and it never reached a vote, so no recorded party split ever existed; opposition is only visible in the absence of any committee or floor action.

industries.industry: Owners and executives of companies facing mass-tort lawsuits
industries.note: The bill takes away their ability to emerge from a company's bankruptcy free of government claims against them personally. Its name points at the Sackler family, whose proposed opioid settlement relied on exactly this kind of release; without the ban, wealthy owners keep an exit that ordinary defendants never have.

Restructuring lawyers and companies lose their most valuable tool for ending mass litigation — the third-party release — at least for government claims. The CRS summary notes courts currently allow the practice and that a circuit split governs when, so a statutory ban reshapes how big corporate bankruptcies are negotiated.
